items.readable_text:
Content:
Up until now, you've been told that you can't take the square root of a negative number. Well, this is actually not entirely true.

Content:
To take the square root of a negative number, we need to expand our domain beyond the real numbers (integers, rationals, and irrationals) to the realm of imaginary numbers.

Content:
The fundamental imaginary number is [MATH: \textrm{i}], which is defined to be the square root of [MATH: -1\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{i} =\sqrt{-1}]

Content:
Following this, we can find the square root of any other negative number, such as [MATH: -9,] as follows:
[MATH: sqrt(− 9)|= sqrt(9 ⋅ (− 1)); = sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(− 1); = 3 ⋅ \textrm{i}; = 3\textrm{i}]

Content:
All other imaginary numbers are multiples of [MATH: \textrm{i}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Up until now, you've been told that you can't take the square root of a negative number. Well, this is actually not entirely true.

Content:
To take the square root of a negative number, we need to expand our domain beyond the real numbers (integers, rationals, and irrationals) to the realm of imaginary numbers.

Content:
The fundamental imaginary number is [MATH: \textrm{i}], which is defined to be the square root of [MATH: -1\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{i} =\sqrt{-1}]

Content:
Following this, we can find the square root of any other negative number, such as [MATH: -9,] as follows:
[MATH: sqrt(− 9)|= sqrt(9 ⋅ (− 1)); = sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(− 1); = 3 ⋅ \textrm{i}; = 3\textrm{i}]

Content:
All other imaginary numbers are multiples of [MATH: \textrm{i}.]

---
